newsitem.title: USA: Advanced Micro to take on Intel with TV advertising campaign.
newsitem.headline: Advanced Micro to take on Intel with TV advertising campaign.

text.p: Advanced Micro Devices Inc., long an also-ran in the computer chip business, will begin an aggressive television campaign next week with a spot during the TV show "Seinfeld" to pitch its speedy new K6 microprocessor -- its first serious threat to Intel Corp.'s Pentium chip.

After two years of engineering and billion-dollar bets on new chip factories, Advanced Micro this week stunned the computer industry by unveiling the K6, a microprocessor for standard PCs that can crunch numbers and handle graphics more quickly than Intel's top-of-the-line Pentium Pro.

But designing a state-of-the-art microprocessor is a piece of cake compared with what Advanced Micro has to do next: Convince consumers that it's okay to buy a PC that does not have the "Intel Inside" sticker.

"I wish them luck," said John Lister, chief executive of Lister Butler Inc., a New York brand-name research firm. "The advice I would offer to AMD is that they better be ready to spend a lot of money and energy to build their brand."
Advanced Micro will have to go against one of the best-known brands, both inside and outside of the computer industry.

Intel, the world's biggest maker of computer chips, has spent millions in the past three years on the "Intel Inside" campaign, even though Intel's chips are the brains of about 90 percent of the world's PCs anyway.

Intel's campaign has been so successful, in fact, that it has irked some of the biggest computer companies, including Compaq Computer Corp. and International Business Machines Corp. The message of the campaign, the PC makers have complained, is that the chip inside is more important than the machine itself.

Consumers seem to agree. Advanced Micro and Cyrix Corp. have long offered microprocessors at a fraction of the price of Intel's chips. But in 1996, non-Intel microprocessor makers had just 5 percent of the $15.4 billion worldwide market for PC microprocessors, according to market researcher Dataquest.

Jerry Sanders, Advanced Micro chairman, said he knows Advanced Micro has a tough task attracting consumers who care about what's under a PC's hood. But consumers and PC makers are ready for an alternative to the Intel monopoly, he said.
"This is about the good guys vs. the bad guys," Sanders said. "It's like the Return of the Jedi. We're the Jedi."

Before the K6, Advanced Micro's microprocessors had been at least three years behind Intel in computing horsepower. It did not have to counter Intel's marketing juggernaut because its customers mainly were second-tier PC makers that bought its chips for low-priced machines.
Two years ago, Advanced Micro gambled its financial future to make sure that the K6 was just as fast, or faster, than comparable Intel chips.

The gamble paid off, at least technically. The K6 beats the Pentium Pro in most everyday applications, according to trade magazines. Not only that, Advanced Micro plans to sell it for at least 25 percent less than the Pentium.

Armed with the K6, Advanced Micro will chase Intel's best customers -- makers of high-end professional and consumer PCs. But first, it has to prove to them that someone will buy a machine that does not have Intel chips inside it.
So far, Advanced Micro has not announced any customers for the K6.
The K6 marketing campaign will focus on the chip's speed without getting esoteric.

At the K6 launch in Sunnyvale, Calif., Sanders showed a trailer of a 30-second, action-packed spot that will appear during next week's "Seinfeld" episode. It featured an 18-wheeler tanker truck rampaging through a downtown street, ramming parked cars along the way and setting off explosions.
The point of the ad is to show "that the K6 is the best engine to run Microsoft Windows," said Scott Allen, Advanced Micro spokesman.

Allen said Advanced Micro does not have the marketing resources to battle Intel on every front, but the company will pick its fights. Advanced Micro will target technology-savvy markets such as San Francisco, Seattle and New York, he said.
